claims.text: Volvo presents the EX30 interior as a minimalist Scandinavian design that deliberately uses renewable and recycled materials (textiles, wool blends, recycled polyester, and bio-based synthetic leather options) and a combined driver/center touchscreen as the cockpit focus.
claims.about: Volvo EX30 interior materials and design

claims.text: Carwow’s 2026 review says the EX30 “looks cool and upmarket” but finds “plenty of cheap materials” and warns that “controlling everything through the screen can be frustrating” and that the speedo being off to the side forces glances away from the road.

Autocar’s 2026 test of the EX30 reports that the car’s driver‑monitoring together with its centralised instrumentation are “the chief culprit” for distraction, saying testers often disabled driver monitoring to stop repeated warnings while looking at the single display.
claims.about: Volvo EX30 instrument layout and distraction

claims.text: Carwow and Auto Express (reviews of the EX30) document early software problems (buggy touchscreen and intermittent keyless‑entry issues) and say OTA updates subsequently improved those issues, i.e., several reviewers reported reliability problems with early software versions.

BMW’s F70 1 Series (marketed from 2024/25) adopts a curved dual display and a largely button‑free cockpit with BMW Operating System 9 and offers leather‑free Veganza and recycled textile seat options as standard/available trims.
claims.about: BMW 1 Series (F70) interior materials and digital cockpit

claims.text: Contemporary reviews of the F70 note BMW’s curved display and removal of many physical controls (including the iDrive controller), and while reviewers often call the interface snappier they also flag missing tactile controls and small interaction quirks (e.g., no dedicated nav button), which can make operation less ‘no‑look’ and potentially more distracting for some drivers.

Inference (based on the cited reviews): compared with the BMW F70—whose cabin emphasizes a curved-glass digital display and Veganza/leather‑free surfaces to create a contemporary premium feel—the EX30 emphasizes visible recycled and bio‑based materials and a spare Scandinavian layout but reviewers note some lower‑cost plastics and a heavier reliance on a single touchscreen, making the EX30 feel more explicitly sustainability‑driven while the BMW aims for a more traditionally ‘premium’ digital finish; this inference is drawn from the Volvo EX30 reviews (Carwow, Autocar, MotorTrend) and BMW F70 press/reviews (Motor1, BMWBLOG).
claims.publisher: Inference citing Carwow, Autocar, MotorTrend, Motor1, BMWBLOG
claims.about: Comparative inference: EX30 vs BMW 1er (F70) interior materials and design
